strengths: Originality: The statistical formulation connects image resolution, template separation, and deformation complexity in a useful way. Its contribution lies in this theoretical perspective, with appropriate connections to pattern theory and functional data analysis.

Significance: The efficient support-alignment classifier and its approximation analysis (Lemma A.7 and Theorem 3.6) explain why very few labeled examples can suffice under a noiseless scaling-and-translation model. This provides an informative benchmark.
Presentation: The modeling assumptions and classifier constructions are explained clearly, with helpful illustrations and extensive proof appendices.

Limitations and ethics: The manuscript openly discusses computationally intractable optimization, background noise, partial visibility, and multiple objects. These acknowledgments appropriately delimit the contribution. The theoretical study and MNIST experiments raise no apparent material ethical concerns.
weaknesses: Soundness—CNN learning objective: Equation (27) minimizes -(1/n)∑ k_i 1(q_2(X_i)>1/2), which is not empirical misclassification error for labels in {0,1}: class-0 errors incur no penalty. The constant class-1 classifier is always a minimizer and has population error 1−π, contradicting Theorem 4.1's vanishing bound. The claimed equivalence to classification ERM in equation (94) is therefore false. The objective must be corrected before the oracle inequality applies.

Soundness—general inverse-mapping guarantee: Lemma A.3 establishes approximation to the normalized template for a suitable inverse B*. However, the proof of Theorem 3.1 on page 29 applies that bound to arbitrary B_i and B when lower-bounding distances between different classes. This existential-to-uniform inference is invalid. Since classifier (10) minimizes over all candidate inverses, controlling only suitable inverses does not establish perfect classification. A separation argument covering every candidate composition is missing.

Soundness—claimed optimal separation: Theorem 3.7 constructs indistinguishable pixel observations with raw L2 template distance of order 1/d. The upper guarantees instead require separation D after minimizing over brightness and geometric transformations, as defined in (12) or (21). A lower bound on raw L2 distance does not imply a lower bound on D. The construction therefore does not establish the claimed matching optimality without an additional argument controlling separation after transformations.

Presentation and theorem consistency: Theorem 4.2, Lemma 4.3, and Proposition B.4 reference the scaling-and-translation separation in (21), whereas Theorem 4.1 and the CNN proof use the general deformation separation in (12). These quantities are not interchangeable for rotations or nonlinear deformations. The theorem statements need consistent assumptions.

Significance and empirical support: Section 5 illustrates alignment on a narrow synthetic setting but does not substantiate the CNN rate or resolution-dependent claims. Experiments fix d=28, use n≤64, and evaluate CNN architectures with local pooling that differ from the analyzed construction. There is no resolution sweep, separation measurement, or evaluation of the broader nonlinear deformation model. Medians over 30 repetitions with 100 test examples are reported without variability. Even after correcting (27), an exact-ERM guarantee would not establish the behavior of the Adam-trained networks used here.

Reproducibility: The manuscript provides architecture descriptions and the optimizer learning rate, but omits deformation ranges and distributions, template identifiers, interpolation and boundary settings, training loss, epochs, batch sizes, and random seeds. No code link is supplied. These details materially affect the small-sample comparisons and prevent reliable reproduction from the manuscript.
